To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) life-narrative is a powerful tool for healing and strengthening personal (and group, community, and society) subjectivity in the context of trauma; 2) a Eucharistic theology of remembrance is a powerful tool in healing and strengthening personal and communal subjectivity in the midst of the traumatic and the monstrous; and 3) the combination of these two practices is a powerful tool to heal and strengthen personal, communal, and societal subjectivity and identity.

1) the concept of the "interior force of being" is a viable and useful concept in the study of trauma and healing; 2) a Eucharistic ritual that commemorates the trauma and suffering of the enslaved is a powerful tool for healing and redemption in the context of the American democracy experiment; and 3) the practice of creating personal life-narratives, in the context of Eucharistic ritual, is an effective tool in the healing process of those suffering from trauma
the practice of creating a life narrative is a therapeutic tool that can precipitate healing in those who have experienced trauma.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a practical/theology that can be used in a variety of ways in the context of theological education, faith communities, and society at large to address the trauma of the past and to help us imagine a more just future.
a theological anthropology that is informed by the interior force of life and the Eucharistic hermenutic of the grotesque and the traumatic.
how to make sense of the trauma and the grotesque in our lives and the lives of others, and how to create a space for remembering and lamenting the trauma and the atrocities that have occurred.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this chapter is a practical and public theological call to the Church to engage with the practice of creating and telling life-narratives as a way of healing and strengthening the subjectivity of the oppressed and marginalized.
this chapter is about the need to remember the past, lament the pain, and ritualize the process of healing in order for the democracy experiment to be redeemed.
a theology and praxis of remembering and lament is necessary in order to address personal, cultural and societal trauma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have sought to demonstrate that the interior force of Being, as it is revealed in the lived experience of the black church, is the very force that is needed to redeem the democracy experiment in the United States.
the project is an invitation to remember the trauma that has been inflicted on the marginalized and oppressed, and to lament the ways that the trauma has become a part of the collective unconscious.

the practice of life-story telling and the ritual of Eucharistic remembrance and lament are two ways of addressing the trauma of the past and the present that is entrenched in the interspace between self and other.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the practice of remembering and lamenting is a necessary and important component in the process of redeeming the democratic experiment.

the practice of creating and sharing life-narratives is a form of resistance that is necessary for healing, and that the practice of remembering and lament is a form of public ritual that is necessary for a healthy democracy.
the practice of creating and telling life-narratives is a powerful tool for healing and for strengthening the personal subjectivity of those who have suffered.
